title: How the Kowloon Walled City Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Kowloon Walled City in Hong Kong, a densely packed, largely unregulated settlement that grew from a Qing-era military fort wall. They trace its origins to the First Opium War and the 1898 lease that left the walled area as Chinese territory within British Hong Kong, the squatting and refugee influx after World War II, the Kai Tak Airport connection, and its unusual vertical, interconnected buildings. They describe daily life (leaking pipes, trash-netted alleys, unlicensed dentists, triad control, schools, factories), the 1987 census and resettlement deal, the final eviction and demolition in 1992 to 1994, and its afterlife as a park and in films and games. The episode closes with a listener mail exchange about Ernest Shackleton's nationality.

segments.title: Opening banter and show intro
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the show's meaning of its title and banter about tea and movies.

segments.title: Density of the Kowloon Walled City
segments.summary: The hosts compare the population density of the walled city with the East Village in New York and describe its size, roughly six and a half acres with about 500 buildings and up to fourteen stories.

segments.title: Interconnected buildings and visual impressions
segments.summary: The buildings were so close that makeshift bridges linked them, making the settlement look like one organism; the hosts reference Ready Player One and Blade Runner.

segments.title: Pop culture tangents
segments.summary: Banter about the animated film Flow and movies like Howards End and Far and Away.

segments.title: Opium Wars and origins of the walled fort
segments.summary: The First Opium War between Britain and Qing China led to Hong Kong ceded land; the Qing built a fifteen-foot-thick wall on the Kowloon Peninsula housing about 150 soldiers, which gave the settlement its name.
topics: origin of the name Kowloon Walled City

segments.title: Second Convention of Peking and the 1898 lease
segments.summary: Treaties from the Second Opium War led to the ninety-nine-year British lease of Hong Kong, while the walled city area was kept as Chinese territory.

segments.title: Chinese sovereignty over the walled area
segments.summary: A clause left the walled city as a small Chinese-held enclave within the British territory.

segments.title: Squatters, Japanese occupation, and post-war evictions
segments.summary: Squatters, including Christian missionaries and pig farmers, moved in; Japanese forces tore down the walls to build Kai Tak Airport; after World War II refugees resettled and the British evicted squatters in 1948, but they returned.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Chinese Civil War refugees and China's support
segments.summary: Refugees from the Chinese Civil War settled in the city; mainland China supported them, and China used the enclave to pressure Britain.

segments.title: Unregulated growth, building code, lovers buildings, and sunlight
segments.summary: British hands-off approach let the city grow with only a fourteen-story height limit; buildings tipped into each other as lovers buildings; sunlight barely reached streets, and flat prices are mentioned.

segments.title: Utilities, costs, and everyday hazards
segments.summary: Residents tapped public utilities informally, avoided business taxes, and dealt with leaking pipes and trash-netted alleys.

segments.title: Economy, unlicensed services, schools, and triad order
segments.summary: Hundreds of businesses operated including factories, unlicensed dentists and doctors, schools, rooftop gardens, pigeon racing, volunteer services, and triad-run order and crime including heroin and brothels.

segments.title: Triad rule and the gray-area view
segments.summary: Hosts discuss triad rule as a substitute for police, with an anecdote about a neighborhood drug dealer, and conclude the place should be neither vilified nor romanticized.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Second mid-episode break.

segments.title: Return and banter
segments.summary: Hosts return with banter about the Ninety Nine Percent Invisible episode and a Brunswick stew idiom.

segments.title: Tung Tao Estate resettlement and the 1898 lease deadline
segments.summary: In 1962 the government built the Tung Tao Estate for resettlement; residents formed an anti-demolition committee, China protested, and the approaching 1997 handover pushed Britain to negotiate secretly from 1986.

segments.title: 1987 census and final resettlement agreement
segments.summary: Officials conducted a census in January 1987 and China formally agreed to give the city to Britain for clearance; residents were offered compensation and high-rise housing; holdouts persisted due to pride.

segments.title: Final eviction, demolition, and park
segments.summary: The last resident left in July 1992 after protests; the city was demolished by 1994 and Kai Tak Airport was moved, and the site became a park retaining the original office's footprint.

segments.title: Film depictions and Bloodsport
segments.summary: The city inspired films and games, including Bloodsport, with hosts briefly chatting about Jean-Claude Van Damme.
topics: films inspired by Kowloon Walled City

segments.title: Listener mail on Shackleton's nationality
segments.summary: A listener, Jamie Finnegan, rebuts an earlier mail about Ernest Shackleton being described as British; the hosts read both emails and leave the question open.
